course: Basic First Aid for Business and Community

lessons.title: Heat Exhaustion and Heat Stroke
lessons.body:
Heat exhaustion and heat stroke are common in hot African climates, especially for outdoor workers, market vendors, and athletes. Heat exhaustion signs include heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache, and muscle cramps. Body temperature may be normal or slightly high (up to 39Â°C). Move the person to a cool, shaded area, loosen tight clothing, and give cool water or oral rehydration salts (ORS) if they are fully conscious. Fan them and apply cool wet cloths to the neck, armpits, and groin. If symptoms worsen or last more than an hour, seek medical help.

Heat stroke is a life-threatening emergency. The person's core temperature rises above 40Â°C, and their skin may be hot, dry, or sweaty. They may become confused, slur their speech, have seizures, or become unconscious. Call for emergency help immediately. While waiting, start rapid cooling: move to shade, remove excess clothing, pour cool water over the body, fan vigorously, and place ice packs or cold wet cloths on the neck, armpits, and groin. Do not give fluids if the person is unconscious or confused. Cooling must begin within minutes to prevent organ damage or death.

Prevention is key: drink water every 15-20 minutes even if not thirsty, avoid alcohol and sugary drinks, wear light-colored loose clothing, and schedule heavy work for cooler times of day. In many African communities, ORS is available at pharmacies and health centers. Learn to recognize early signs and act fast. Remember: heat stroke is a medical emergencyâcool first, transport second. For business owners, ensure workers have access to shade, water, and rest breaks. This simple step can save lives and keep productivity high.

lessons.title: Hypothermia and Frostbite
lessons.body:
Hypothermia occurs when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, causing core temperature to drop below 35Â°C. In Africa, it can happen in high-altitude areas like Mount Kilimanjaro, the Drakensberg, or the Atlas Mountains, and even during cold nights in deserts. Signs include shivering, cold pale skin, confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness, and slow breathing. If untreated, shivering stops and the person may become unconscious. Move the person to a warm, dry place, remove wet clothing, and wrap them in blankets or dry clothes. Warm the core first: apply warm compresses to the neck, chest, and groin. Give warm, sweet drinks if they are conscious. Do not rub the skin or give alcohol. Seek medical help immediately.

Frostbite is freezing of skin and underlying tissues, usually on fingers, toes, ears, and nose. It starts with numbness, then skin turns white or grayish-yellow, feels hard, and may blister. Do not rub the area with snow or massage it. Instead, move the person to a warm place and gently rewarm the affected part in warm water (37-39Â°C) for 20-30 minutes. Do not use direct heat like fire or heaters. If blisters form, cover loosely with sterile gauze. Do not pop blisters. Get medical help.

Prevention: wear layered clothing, gloves, hats, and waterproof boots in cold conditions. Keep dry and avoid wind. In high-altitude trekking, carry emergency blankets. For business owners in cold regions, provide warm shelters and hot drinks. Early recognition and gentle rewarming are critical. Never rub frostbitten skinâit can cause permanent damage.

lessons.title: Cold Water Immersion and Drowning Response
lessons.body:
Cold water immersion can quickly lead to hypothermia and drowning, even in warm climates. In Africa, this can happen in cold lakes like Lake Tanganyika or during floods. When someone falls into cold water, they may gasp and inhale water, leading to drowning. Cold shock response includes rapid breathing, increased heart rate, and panic. If you see someone in trouble, do not jump in unless trained. Instead, reach with a pole, throw a rope or floatation device, or row a boat. Call for help. If you must enter, wear a life jacket.

For drowning response, get the person out of the water safely. Check for responsiveness and breathing. If not breathing, start CPR immediately: 30 chest compressions (push hard and fast at 100-120 per minute) followed by 2 rescue breaths. If you are not trained in rescue breaths, do hands-only CPR. Continue until help arrives or the person breathes. If the person is breathing but unconscious, place them in the recovery position (on their side) to keep the airway clear. Do not try to drain water from the lungsâit wastes time. Keep the person warm to prevent hypothermia. Even if they seem fine, seek medical help because complications can develop.

Prevention: learn to swim, wear life jackets, avoid alcohol around water, and supervise children. In flood-prone areas, move to higher ground. For business owners near water, provide life jackets and train staff in basic water rescue. Remember: drowning is silent and fast. Act immediately.

lessons.title: Lightning and Electrical Injuries
lessons.body:
Lightning strikes and electrical injuries can cause severe burns, cardiac arrest, and neurological damage. In Africa, lightning is common during rainy seasons, especially in highlands. If you are outdoors during a storm, seek shelter in a building or a hard-topped vehicle. Avoid tall trees, open fields, water, and metal objects. If caught in the open, crouch down with feet together, head low, and minimize contact with the ground. Do not lie flat. If someone is struck by lightning, they do not carry an electrical chargeâit is safe to touch them. Call for help. Check for breathing and pulse. If not breathing, start CPR immediately. Treat burns with cool water and sterile dressings. Seek medical help even if the person seems okay, as effects can be delayed.

Electrical injuries from power lines or faulty wiring are also common. Do not touch the person if they are still in contact with the electrical source. Turn off the power at the main switch or use a dry wooden stick to separate them. Once safe, check breathing and pulse. Start CPR if needed. Treat burns by covering with a clean, dry cloth. Do not apply ointments or ice. Seek medical attention for all electrical injuries, as internal damage may be severe.

Prevention: install lightning rods on buildings, avoid using corded phones during storms, and teach children about electrical safety. In businesses, ensure wiring is up to code and avoid overloading sockets. For rural communities, lightning safety education is vital. Remember: lightning can strike twice in the same place. Stay indoors until 30 minutes after the last thunder.

lessons.title: Animal Bites, Stings, and Snakebites
lessons.body:
Animal bites, stings, and snakebites are common in many African communities. For any bite that breaks the skin, wash the wound gently with soap and water for at least 5 minutes. Apply an antibiotic ointment if available and cover with a sterile bandage. Seek medical help for rabies and tetanus prevention, especially for dog, bat, or wild animal bites. Rabies is fatal if untreated, so do not delay. For snakebites, keep the person calm and still. Remove tight clothing or jewelry near the bite. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. Immobilize the limb and keep it below heart level. Note the time of the bite and any symptoms like swelling, difficulty breathing, or drooping eyelids. Get to a hospital with antivenom as quickly as possible. If you can safely identify the snake, take a photo, but do not risk another bite.

For insect stings (bees, wasps, scorpions), remove the stinger by scraping with a credit card or fingernail. Wash with soap and water. Apply a cold pack to reduce swelling. For scorpion stings, seek medical help immediately, especially for children. Watch for signs of allergic reaction: difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, rapid pulse, or hives. If these occur, use an epinephrine auto-injector if available and call for emergency help. If not, get to a hospital immediately.

Prevention: wear boots and long pants when walking in tall grass, use insect repellent, and shake out shoes and clothing before wearing. For business owners, keep first aid kits stocked with antiseptics, bandages, and antihistamines. Train staff in basic bite and sting response. Remember: time is critical for snakebites and severe allergic reactions.

lessons.title: Poisoning and Toxic Exposure
lessons.body:
Poisoning can happen from swallowing, inhaling, or touching toxic substances. Common causes in Africa include paraffin, pesticides, household cleaners, and carbon monoxide from charcoal stoves. If someone swallows poison, do not induce vomiting unless told by a medical professional. For corrosive substances (like bleach or battery acid), give small sips of water or milk to dilute, but only if the person is conscious and not having seizures. Call a poison control center or seek emergency help immediately. Note the substance and amount. If the person is unconscious, place them in the recovery position and monitor breathing. If they stop breathing, start CPR.

For inhaled poisons like carbon monoxide, move the person to fresh air immediately. Open windows and doors. If they are not breathing, start CPR. For skin contact, remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin with soap and water for 15-20 minutes. For eye exposure, flush the eye with clean water for 15-20 minutes, holding the eyelid open. Do not use any neutralizers. Seek medical help.

Prevention: store all chemicals in original labeled containers, out of reach of children. Never store paraffin or pesticides in drink bottles. Use charcoal stoves in well-ventilated areas. Install carbon monoxide detectors if possible. For businesses, train staff on safe handling of chemicals and provide protective gear. Keep a first aid kit with activated charcoal only if advised by a professional. Remember: when in doubt, call for help and bring the container or label to the hospital. Quick action saves lives.

quiz.q: What is a key sign of heat exhaustion?
quiz.explanation: Heat exhaustion often causes heavy sweating, weakness, and dizziness, while heat stroke may cause hot dry skin and unconsciousness.

quiz.q: What should you do first for someone with heat stroke?
options: A) Give them water to drink
B) Move them to a cool area and start cooling
C) Make them walk to the clinic
quiz.explanation: Rapid cooling is critical for heat stroke; move to shade and apply cool water and fanning.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of hypothermia?
quiz.explanation: Hypothermia causes shivering, confusion, and cold pale skin as body temperature drops.

quiz.q: How should you rewarm a frostbitten area?
options: B) Use direct heat like a fire
quiz.explanation: Frostbite should be rewarmed gently in warm water, not rubbed or exposed to direct heat.

quiz.q: What is the first step when someone is drowning and not breathing?
options: A) Try to drain water from lungs
quiz.explanation: CPR should be started immediately for a drowning victim who is not breathing; do not waste time trying to drain water.

quiz.q: If you are caught outdoors in a lightning storm, what should you do?
options: A) Lie flat on the ground
B) Stand under a tall tree
C) Crouch down with feet together
quiz.explanation: Crouching with feet together minimizes ground contact and reduces risk of lightning injury.

quiz.q: What should you do if someone is in contact with a live electrical wire?
options: A) Pull them away with your hands
B) Turn off the power source first
D) Use a metal pole to separate them
quiz.explanation: Always turn off the power before touching the person to avoid electrocution.

quiz.q: How should you treat a snakebite?
options: A) Cut the wound and suck out venom
C) Keep the person calm and immobilize the limb
quiz.explanation: Keep the person calm, immobilize the bitten limb below heart level, and get to a hospital with antivenom.

quiz.q: What is the correct first aid for a bee sting?
options: B) Scrape the stinger with a card
quiz.explanation: Scraping the stinger prevents squeezing more venom into the skin.

quiz.q: What should you do if someone swallows a corrosive poison?
options: B) Give large amounts of water
C) Give small sips of water or milk if conscious
quiz.explanation: For corrosive poisons, dilute with small sips of water or milk if the person is conscious, but do not induce vomiting.

quiz.q: What is a sign of severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)?
options: B) Difficulty breathing and swelling of face
quiz.explanation: Anaphylaxis causes difficulty breathing, facial swelling, and requires immediate epinephrine and emergency care.

quiz.q: How long should you flush an eye exposed to chemicals?
quiz.explanation: Flush the eye with clean water for at least 15-20 minutes to remove the chemical.

quiz.q: What is the recommended compression rate for CPR?
quiz.explanation: CPR compressions should be at a rate of 100-120 per minute for effective circulation.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a prevention measure for heat stroke?
options: A) Drink alcohol to cool down
D) Work during hottest part of day
quiz.explanation: Frequent water intake helps prevent dehydration and heat-related illnesses.

quiz.q: What should you do for someone with hypothermia who is conscious?
options: D) Place them in a cold bath
quiz.explanation: Warm sweet drinks help raise core temperature; alcohol and rubbing can worsen the condition.

quiz.q: What is the first step when you see someone drowning?
options: B) Call for help and throw a floatation device
C) Wait for them to stop struggling
quiz.explanation: Reach or throw a floatation device; only trained rescuers should enter the water.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a safe practice during a lightning storm?
options: B) Stay in a hard-topped vehicle
quiz.explanation: A hard-topped vehicle provides a safe shelter from lightning.

quiz.q: What should you do for a scorpion sting?
quiz.explanation: Scorpion stings can be dangerous, especially for children, and require immediate medical attention.

quiz.q: How should you handle a dog bite that breaks the skin?
options: A) Wash with soap and water for 5 minutes
B) Cover with a dirty cloth
quiz.explanation: Thorough washing reduces infection risk; seek medical help for rabies and tetanus prevention.

quiz.q: What is a common source of carbon monoxide poisoning in African homes?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal stoves produce carbon monoxide; use them in well-ventilated areas.

quiz.q: What should you do if someone is unconscious but breathing after a drowning incident?
options: A) Place them in recovery position
quiz.explanation: Recovery position keeps the airway clear and prevents choking if they vomit.

quiz.q: Which is a sign of frostbite?
quiz.explanation: Frostbitten skin turns white or grayish-yellow and feels hard and numb.

quiz.q: What is the correct action for a snakebite if the snake is dead?
options: A) Bring the snake to the hospital
B) Take a photo if safe
quiz.explanation: A photo helps identify the snake for proper antivenom, but do not risk another bite by handling it.

quiz.q: What should you do for a chemical burn on the skin?
options: B) Wash with soap and water for 15-20 minutes
C) Cover with a bandage immediately
quiz.explanation: Remove contaminated clothing and flush the skin with soap and water for 15-20 minutes.

quiz.q: What is the first aid for a person struck by lightning?
options: A) Do not touch them because they are charged
B) Check breathing and start CPR if needed
quiz.explanation: Lightning victims do not carry a charge; check breathing and start CPR if necessary.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a prevention measure for poisoning?
options: A) Store chemicals in drink bottles
B) Keep chemicals out of reach of children
quiz.explanation: Store all chemicals safely out of reach of children and in original labeled containers.

quiz.q: What should you do if someone has heat cramps?
options: B) Move to cool area and give ORS
quiz.explanation: Heat cramps are treated with rest in a cool place and oral rehydration salts.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to remove a tick?
options: A) Burn it with a match
B) Pull it straight out with tweezers
C) Cover it with petroleum jelly
quiz.explanation: Use fine-tipped tweezers to pull the tick straight out close to the skin; do not burn or squeeze.

quiz.q: What should you do for a person with severe hypothermia who is unconscious?
options: B) Start CPR and handle gently
quiz.explanation: Handle the person gently and start CPR if not breathing; avoid rough movements that can cause cardiac arrest.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of heat stroke?
options: A) Heavy sweating with cool skin
quiz.explanation: Heat stroke causes confusion, hot skin, and body temperature above 40Â°C.
